data.title: WSJ Tech Council Summit: NASA's Isaacman Wants Agency to Get Back Its Mojo
data.description:
By Elias Schisgall 




  Jared Isaacman wants the National Aeronautics and Space Administration to regain its mojo. 



  The NASA administrator said the agency has lost its focus and ability to quickly execute in recent years. "We are just trying to get our swagger back here, get back in a rhythm of what we did" in the 1960s, Isaacman said at The Wall Street Journal's Technology Council Summit, calling that period NASA's "glory days." 



  "This is simply going back to the playbook that achieved these near-impossible outcomes from decades past," Isaacman said. 



  There is urgency, he said, to breathe life into the agency as the U.S. races China to establish a presence on the moon and secure valuable lunar real estate. 



  "There is a second space race. It will come down to months, not years. The Chinese will absolutely put their astronauts on the surface of the Moon, do what the Soviets never could," Isaacman said. "And I think the implications of that will be felt around the world." 



  Isaacman has tried to realize this shift by eliminating "needless bureaucracy" and flattening the agency's organizational structure, as well as by spending more time in the field himself. 



  He is also trying to bring more of NASA's workforce back in-house, after what he described as an extended period of outsourcing to contractors that contributed to higher costs and slower launch cadences. 



  Personnel for mission control and rocket designing, construction and launching should be brought within the agency, Isaacman said. And though NASA should continue to act as one customer of many for components and services that have a high level of technical readiness, he said the agency should be more hands-on for more ambitious projects, such as spacecraft fueled by nuclear power. 



  "We are course-correcting back to center on the balance between, what is the near-impossible--it doesn't have an obvious business or use case--that NASA should be doing, and where can you leverage industry to supplement, just as we did in the early days," Isaacman said. "I think we're getting back to the right balance there."

data.title: 2 charts showing how oil is becoming the market's biggest wild card
data.description:
By Isabel Wang

Crude is increasingly 'the straw that stirs the drink' of the current global macro risk regime, a Nomura strategist warns

Oil is becoming a bigger problem for both stocks and long-term bonds.

Oil is increasingly calling the tune in global markets, as rising energy prices and worries about how much consumers are paying at the gas pump are making investors nervous and affecting their portfolios.

Since the U.S.-Iran war began in late February, higher oil prices have been bad news for both stocks and long-term Treasury bonds. When crude prices jump, stocks tend to fall. The same is true for long-duration government debt, as higher oil prices have been accompanied by falling bond prices and, in turn, higher yields.

That relationship has become much stronger over the past seven months, as shown in the charts below.

The Iran war appears to have marked a turning point in the relationship between oil and both stocks and Treasurys. Before the war, the relationship between U.S. benchmark West Texas Intermediate crude (CL00) (CL.1) (CLV26) and the S&P 500 SPX was basically neutral, with their rolling 63-day correlation at just 0.04 on Feb. 27. But by the end of March, it had fallen to minus 0.35, and by late April it had reached minus 0.48, according to Dow Jones Market Data. In other words, when oil prices rise, stocks have increasingly tended to fall.

A value closer to minus 1 means a perfect negative correlation between oil prices and stocks, while a number closer to 0 shows the relationship is very weak or even nonexistent.

The same pattern is showing up in long-term Treasurys. The rolling 63-day correlation between the U.S. oil benchmark and the iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF TLT fell to minus 0.28 by the end of April, from minus 0.15 on Feb. 27. It was at minus 0.55 on Tuesday morning, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

"Crude oil and energy is 'the straw that stirs the drink' of the current global macro risk regime," said Charlie McElligott, cross-asset macro strategist at Nomura Securities International.

Indeed, oil is increasingly behaving like a macro risk for equities, rather than simply another indicator of economic growth. Normally, higher oil prices can be bullish for stocks because they can signal stronger economic demand. That's partly why the correlation between WTI and the S&P 500 was mostly positive in 2025.

But now, the oil supply shock brought on by the Middle East conflict is propelling energy prices higher as transportation and production costs rise. At the same time, central banks are fighting to keep interest rates higher for longer. That matters to U.S. households because higher rates would directly increase the cost of borrowing money for mortgages, car loans and credit cards. They can also eat into American businesses' bottom lines, squeezing corporate margins and weighing on equity valuations.

"Treasury yields are now impacted less by safe-haven flows and more by inflation expectations, and the correlation between yields and oil prices is at its highest level for seven years," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB.

In other words, the oil shock is having a direct impact on U.S. financial conditions, Brooks told MarketWatch on Tuesday.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury note BX:TMUBMUSD10Y was up 2 basis points Tuesday to trade at 5.040%, its highest intraday level since July 19, 2007. The 30-year Treasury rate BX:TMUBMUSD30Y was also up 2 basis points, at 5.369%, according to FactSet data.

"I've always found it somewhat odd that front-month oil correlates so highly to the 10-year Treasury [yield], but their increasingly synchronized moves reflect not only [that] inflation is at risk but real rates are backing up substantially," said Nate Shetty, chief investment officer at SEI Investments Company.

Real interest rates are nominal interest rates minus the inflation rate. When they rise substantially, it means money is genuinely becoming more expensive to borrow for U.S. consumers and businesses in terms of actual purchasing power.

"We are believers that Treasurys have lost their flight-to-quality positions," Shetty told MarketWatch in a phone interview on Tuesday. "In other words, the negative correlation we've seen in 20 years past between Treasurys and stocks has now flipped to the positive."

"Another way of saying this is that Treasurys are going to trade like risk assets, and in fact, they are," he said.

Of course, equities won't escape rising oil prices unscathed. "When the consequences of a geopolitical crisis roils oil markets and bruises the bond market, it is only a matter of time before equities get hit," Brooks of XTB added.

Opinion: Stocks have so far survived rising Treasury yields. But that may be about to change.

But aside from this week's tech selloff following calls from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and other executives to slow artificial-intelligence development, U.S. stocks have been resilient. The Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA was off just 0.4% so far this quarter, while the S&P 500 has risen 1.2% and the Nasdaq Composite COMP was down 0.9%, according to FactSet data.

-Isabel Wang

data.title: Merit Coffee Earns Two Gold Medals at the 2026 Global Coffee Awards
data.description:
Merit Coffee Earns Two Gold Medals at the 2026 Global Coffee Awards

Merit Coffee Earns Two Gold Medals at the 2026 Global Coffee Awards

PR Newswire

SAN ANTONIO, Sept. 15, 2026

SAN ANTONIO, Sept. 15, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Merit Coffee Company, the Texas specialty coffee roaster known for its community-driven cafés and award-winning coffee program, has been awarded two gold medals at the 2026 Global Coffee Awards, an international competition recognizing excellence in coffee quality and roasting.

The two gold-medal-winning coffees include Lucem, Merit's "everyday blend," and a limited-edition Peru Gesha Natural that will debut as part of the company's upcoming holiday coffee rollout. Both coffees received top recognition following a rigorous double-blind evaluation by an international panel of certified coffee professionals.

Merit's Lucem Brand has become a signature part of Merit's coffee program and is one of the company's most widely available coffees. Utilizing coffees sourced from Honduras and Brazil, Lucem is sold across all 15 Merit cafés and is also available throughout Texas at retail partners including select H-E-B's, Whole Foods Market, Sprouts, Kroger, and Central Market. Lucem can also be ordered on Merit's online shop at MeritCoffee.com.

The second gold medal was awarded to a Peru Gesha Natural, offering an early glimpse at one of the coffees Merit will introduce during its holiday coffee rollout. The coffee will be released later this year, with additional details regarding its sourcing, character, and availability to be announced closer to its debut.

Both award winning coffees were roasted by Merit's Head Roaster & Q Grader, Carlos Riaño, who recently qualified for the United States Coffee Roasting Championship and will compete this December for a chance to advance to the global finals.

The Global Coffee Awards evaluates coffees solely on sensory quality, with judges assessing attributes including aroma, flavor, balance, sweetness, acidity, body, and overall cup performance. The competition also recognizes the collaborative work of producers and roasters in bringing exceptional coffees from farm to cup.

The two gold medals underscore Merit's continued commitment to sourcing exceptional coffees and thoughtfully roasting each coffee to highlight its unique qualities. The recognition also celebrates both a coffee that customers already know and love and an award-winning coffee that will soon make its way into their cups.

In addition to the two gold medals, five additional Merit coffees received bronze medals, bringing the company's total recognition at the 2026 Global Coffee Awards to seven medals. Camino de Oro, Patlanalan Community, Saddle Up, and Sugarcane Decaf were among the additional Merit coffees recognized, further highlighting the breadth and quality of the company's coffee program.

Additional details regarding the release of the Peru Gesha Natural and Merit's holiday coffee lineup will be announced through Merit Coffee's social media channels and website in the coming months.

About Merit Coffee

Founded in San Antonio in 2009, Merit Coffee is a Texas specialty coffee company dedicated to sourcing, roasting, and serving exceptional coffee. With cafés across San Antonio, Austin, Dallas, and Houston, Merit is committed to creating welcoming spaces where quality coffee, genuine hospitality, and community come together. Merit's coffees are available online, in cafés, and through retail partners across Texas.

Media Contact:
Charlie Paulette
charlie@meritcoffee.com

View original content to download multimedia:https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/merit-coffee-earns-two-gold-medals-at-the-2026-global-coffee-awards-302879709.html

SOURCE Merit Coffee
